questions.q: What does AWS's pay-as-you-go pricing model mean?
options: You're billed for actual usage across dimensions like compute, storage, and data transfer, with no upfront purchase or fixed seat count
Every AWS account pays a fixed monthly fee regardless of usage
AWS charges a one-time lifetime fee per account
Pricing is negotiated individually and never usage-based
questions.explain: Pay-as-you-go is billing tied directly to actual measured usage, not a subscription seat count.

questions.q: Why does an idle EC2 instance still cost money while an empty S3 bucket costs essentially nothing?
options: EC2 bills for the instance running regardless of activity, while S3 bills primarily on data actually stored, and an empty bucket stores nothing
EC2 is always more expensive than S3 for every workload, with no exceptions
S3 buckets are entirely free forever regardless of usage
EC2 instances cannot be stopped once started
questions.explain: This distinction is explicit in the lesson: compute bills for running time, storage bills for what's actually stored.

questions.q: What are the two main kinds of AWS Free Tier allowances described in this lesson?
options: 12-months-free allowances for new accounts, and always-free allowances with a smaller cap that never expire
A single unlimited allowance that never expires for any service
A one-time $100 credit with no usage restrictions
Allowances that only apply to AWS Support plans, not actual services
questions.explain: The Free Tier splits into 12-months-free, always-free, and short trials — bounded, not unlimited.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a Reserved Instance/Savings Plan and a Spot Instance?
options: Reserved/Savings Plans trade a 1-3 year usage commitment for a meaningful discount; Spot trades the risk of interruption for the steepest discount available
Spot Instances require a multi-year commitment while Reserved Instances do not
Reserved Instances are always more expensive than On-Demand pricing
Spot Instances guarantee the instance will never be reclaimed
questions.explain: Both are cost levers over the same underlying compute, but they trade different things (commitment length vs. interruption risk) for discount.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets?
options: Cost Explorer visualizes historical and forecasted spend by service/Region/tag; Budgets lets you set a spend threshold and get alerted when it's crossed
They are the exact same tool under two different names
Budgets only shows historical spend with no alerting capability
Cost Explorer can automatically stop a runaway EC2 instance, while Budgets cannot
questions.explain: Cost Explorer is for visibility into spend; Budgets is the proactive threshold/alerting guardrail.
